sentences.text: Fully grown individuals reached about 5 m in total length.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the body mass at 1.9 tonnes.
The praemaxillae were exceptionally smooth and, in life, were covered by a sheet of horn that formed the upper beak.
Juvenile specimens preserve large paraglossalia that display signs of muscular stress, indicating a muscular tongue common to ankylosaurs.
In juveniles, ribs fused early with vertebrae and the forelimbs became much more robust than the hindlimbs, suggesting the arms bore most of the weight.
The skull bears two to five extra openings beside each nostril, whose function remains unknown.
A thick tail club composed of fused bones served as a defensive weapon.
It differs from distant relatives by having extra nasal fossa openings and a forward-pointing prefrontal caputegula.
Adult skulls measure about 30 cm in length.
The known postcranial skeleton is relatively lightweight, and the holotype of P. mephistocephalus is less than 3 m long.
Fifteen specimens, including a nearly complete skeleton and several skulls, make it the best-known ankylosaurid in the region.
Its diet may have included tough leaves, pulpy fruits, and possibly insects, hinting at a varied or even ant-eater-like feeding style.
The laryngeal cartilages were ossified, showing that laryngeal ossification occurred in some non-avian dinosaurs.
It was likely capable of producing loud, possibly bird-like vocalizations from a non-laryngeal sound organ.
Its relatively light build may have been an adaptation for agility to better confront small, fast theropods, with a tail club fast enough to strike them.
The holotype, specimen AMNH 6523, is a partially crushed skull with lower jaws and dermal plates discovered in 1923 by Walter Wallis Granger.
The most complete skull belongs to a juvenile described by Teresa Maryańska in 1971 and 1977.
Two fossil occurrences of the species have been recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
Pinacosaurus likely relied heavily on a muscular tongue and hyobranchia for feeding because its teeth were small and replaced slowly.
During ontogeny, ribs initially fused to vertebrae and the forelimbs became considerably more robust while the hind limbs did not grow proportionally.
Several groups of juvenile fossils were found together, interpreted as a traveling herd killed by a sandstorm.
Most juvenile skeletons are preserved lying on their backs with legs folded inward.
Pinacosaurus hilwitnorum is placed within the family Ankylosauridae.
It was originally assigned to Nodosauridae but is now considered a member of Ankylosauridae, likely within the subfamily Ankylosaurinae.
It lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
The environment was semi-desert with scattered oases, where only small theropods such as Velociraptor are known.
It inhabited Asia about 80 to 75 million years ago, spanning the Santonian to early Campanian.
More precisely, it lived in the Campanian stage, about 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
The habitat consisted of a semi-desert landscape interspersed with oasis areas.
Gregory S. Paul suggested in 2010 that P. mephistocephalus is a junior synonym of P. grangeri.
